# Three-Week High School Genetics Unit

**15 lessons · 55 minutes each · three performance assessments**

Use one recurring routine: students draw a **genotype → protein or gene expression → phenotype** model in Lesson 1, then revise it when they encounter new evidence. This gives you a quick way to see whether they’re connecting the ideas across weeks rather than treating DNA, inheritance, and phenotype as separate topics.

### Goal and standards key

| Goal | Students will be able to… | NGSS connection |
|---|---|---|
| **G1. DNA and proteins** | Use a model to explain how DNA is copied and how its sequence helps determine the sequence and function of a protein. | **HS-LS1-1:** Construct an evidence-based explanation linking DNA, protein structure, and essential functions. Replication and codon decoding are supporting instruction, not the performance expectation itself. |
| **G2. Inheritance** | Use crosses and pedigrees to predict inheritance, justify a likely pattern, and distinguish known from possible genotypes. | **HS-LS3-1:** Ask questions that clarify the roles of DNA and chromosomes in inheritance. Crosses and pedigrees support this expectation; include student-generated questions as direct evidence. |
| **G3. Inheritance data** | Compare predicted and observed trait distributions using probability and statistics, then explain what the data do and do not support. | **HS-LS3-3:** Apply statistics and probability to variation and the distribution of expressed traits in a population. Chi-square is a unit tool, not an NGSS requirement. |
| **G4. Sources of variation** | Use evidence to explain how mutations and differences in gene expression can affect phenotype, and defend a claim about how heritable variation arises. | **HS-LS3-2:** Make and defend a claim about heritable variation from new allele combinations during meiosis, viable replication errors, and environmentally caused mutations. Protein consequences also support **HS-LS1-1**. |
| **G5. Modeling** | Build and revise a genotype-to-phenotype model, using evidence to justify a revision and identifying a limitation. | Modeling supports **HS-LS1-1** and **HS-LS3-1**; score the explanation and the questions separately from the model itself. |
| **G6. Ethics** | Evaluate evidence and trade-offs in a genetic technology case and defend a recommendation that considers different stakeholders. | An application of NGSS practices for evaluating information and arguing from evidence, with an **ETS1.B** connection. It is not a standalone HS-LS3 performance expectation. |

## Week 1 — From DNA to phenotype

| Day and learning objective | Lesson activity | Materials and resources | 5-minute formative check | Differentiation or extension | Timing |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1. How can a DNA difference affect a trait?** Draw an initial model linking DNA sequence, a protein’s function, and an observable trait. **G1, G5 · HS-LS1-1** | Compare two fictional plant samples with different pigment levels and a data card showing different enzyme activity. Students draw an initial model and mark which links are supported by the evidence and which are still hypotheses. | Plant images; teacher-made enzyme activity card; model template or science notebooks. | **Draw and label:** DNA → protein → trait. Explain one arrow and put a question mark on a link you can’t yet explain. | Provide movable labels and an arrow sentence frame: “A change in ___ could affect ___ because ___.” | 8 launch / 10 evidence / 22 model / 10 compare / 5 exit |
| **2. How is DNA copied?** Use complementary base pairing to model replication and explain how a copying error could create a new allele. **G1, G4 · supports HS-LS1-1 and HS-LS3-2** | Pairs build and copy a short fictional DNA segment using paper strips. They compare an accurate copy with a copy containing one error and discuss why a change in a leaf cell usually would not be passed on through seeds. | Colored paper bases or printed strips; replication handout; optional short HHMI BioInteractive DNA replication animation. | **Copy and explain:** Complete a complementary strand, circle a deliberately mismatched base, and say whether a change confined to a leaf cell would ordinarily be inherited. | Give a base-pair key and lettered strips so students do not have to rely on color. | 5 retrieval / 10 demo / 20 pair model / 15 error discussion / 5 exit |
| **3. How does a DNA sequence affect a protein?** Trace a provided DNA template through mRNA to a short amino acid sequence and explain why sequence matters for protein function. **G1 · HS-LS1-1 support** | Model one worked example, then have partners decode a second short segment. Close by pairing the sequence model with a protein-function evidence card: a codon chart tells you the amino acid sequence, not what the protein will do. | Labeled template and coding strands; mRNA codon chart; worked example; protein-function evidence card. | **Trace and explain:** Given one DNA template triplet, write its mRNA codon and amino acid; identify one thing the codon chart cannot tell you. | Supply a partially completed DNA → mRNA → amino acid table with reading direction marked. | 5 warm-up / 12 modeling / 18 partner practice / 15 evidence discussion / 5 exit |
| **4. Do all mutations change phenotype?** Compare sequence variants and use protein activity and trait data to distinguish predicted effects from observed effects. **G4, G5 · HS-LS1-1; supports HS-LS3-2** | Groups compare an unchanged amino acid sequence, an amino acid substitution, and a frameshift. They revise Day 1 models after receiving activity data and explain why a sequence change alone is not proof of a phenotype change. | Three fictional variant cards; codon chart; sample activity and pigment data; Day 1 models. | **Choose the stronger claim:** “The protein sequence changed” or “The plant’s pigment changed.” Identify the evidence needed to support each. | Give each group one variant first, then use a jigsaw so all students encounter all three. | 5 warm-up / 10 mini-lesson / 20 card analysis / 15 revision / 5 exit |
| **5. Performance assessment 1: Central Dogma Mutation Model.** Construct and defend a model connecting a sequence change to protein function and phenotype, and explain whether the change could be inherited. **G1, G4, G5 · HS-LS1-1; partial evidence for HS-LS3-2** | Students independently annotate a model using a new fictional sequence and a supplied dataset. They write a claim-evidence-reasoning response, note what the data prompted them to revise, and explain how the cell lineage affects heritability. | Assessment packet; short sequences; activity and phenotype data; codon chart; rubric. | **Self-check before submission:** Underline your strongest piece of evidence and star a conclusion your evidence does not let you make. | Offer a blank diagram template with labeled stages, without supplying the connections or conclusions. | 5 launch / 8 plan / 25 model / 12 written explanation / 5 check |

## Week 2 — From family patterns to population distributions

| Day and learning objective | Lesson activity | Materials and resources | 5-minute formative check | Differentiation or extension | Timing |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **6. How do alleles pass from parents to offspring?** Ask a question about how chromosomes carry alleles, then use allele segregation to predict the outcome of a monohybrid cross. **G2 · HS-LS3-1** | Students use chromosome cards to show which allele each parent can pass on, then translate the model into a Punnett square. They compare a prediction for one offspring with an expected proportion across many offspring. | Chromosome and allele cards; monohybrid handout; optional coins. | **Predict and ask:** For `Aa × aa`, give the probability of `aa` and write one question about what happens to the alleles when reproductive cells form. | Keep allele cards beside the Punnett square so students can match each box to a physical combination. | 5 launch / 10 demonstration / 20 model and cross / 15 practice / 5 exit |
| **7. What changes when we track two genes?** Calculate a two-trait probability under independent assortment and state the assumption behind the calculation. **G2, G3 · supports HS-LS3-1 and HS-LS3-3** | Solve one dihybrid problem with a grid and then with the product rule. Compare two samples to illustrate why an expected ratio is not a guarantee for a small group. | Gamete cards; grid and product-rule handout; sample offspring counts. | **Calculate and qualify:** For `AaBb × AaBb`, what is the probability of `aabb` if the genes assort independently? What assumption allows you to multiply? | Give a two-column organizer for the two single-gene probabilities before asking students to combine them. | 5 retrieval / 10 worked example / 20 partner practice / 15 sample comparison / 5 exit |
| **8. What can a pedigree tell us—and what can’t it?** Justify the most likely inheritance pattern using pedigree evidence and distinguish definite from possible genotypes. **G2 · HS-LS3-1** | Groups rotate through fictional autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, and X-linked pedigrees, then examine one deliberately ambiguous case. Each group identifies an additional observation or question that would help distinguish two explanations. | Fictional three-generation pedigrees; symbol key; optional paper allele labels. | **Make the case:** Use one relationship in a mini-pedigree to support a pattern, then mark one individual whose genotype is uncertain. | Start with a partially annotated pedigree, then remove the scaffolding for the ambiguous case. | 5 symbols review / 10 worked case / 20 stations / 15 ambiguous case / 5 exit |
| **9. Why don’t observed ratios match predictions exactly?** Compare simulated trait frequencies with a predicted distribution and interpret a scaffolded chi-square result. **G3 · HS-LS3-3** | Pairs simulate an `Aa × Aa` cross with two coins, then pool their results as a modeled population. Compare pair and class distributions, calculate expected counts, and use a provided critical value to decide whether the class data are inconsistent with the model. | Two coins per pair; tally sheet; calculators or a spreadsheet; chi-square template; backup dataset below. | **Interpret:** “Our result was below the critical value, so we proved the model.” Rewrite the statement and explain why it was too strong. | Provide a completed first row of the chi-square table and a worked example for interpreting the result. | 5 prediction / 8 setup / 15 simulation / 22 analysis / 5 exit |
| **10. Performance assessment 2: Family Inheritance Investigation.** Defend a pedigree interpretation, calculate offspring risk, and use population data to evaluate an inheritance model. **G2, G3 · HS-LS3-1, HS-LS3-3** | Students analyze a new fictional pedigree and a separate simulated population dataset. They write a short letter explaining the family probability and its limits, plus one question about how DNA or chromosomes account for the pattern. | Assessment packet; pedigree; simulated offspring counts; critical-value reference; calculator; rubric. | **Transfer check:** A family has already had two unaffected children. Does that alone change the probability for the next child in your model? Explain. | Offer a letter organizer with prompts for the probability, assumptions, and uncertainty. | 5 launch / 16 pedigree and risk / 16 data analysis / 13 letter and question / 5 exit |

## Week 3 — Variation, gene expression, and decisions

| Day and learning objective | Lesson activity | Materials and resources | 5-minute formative check | Differentiation or extension | Timing |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **11. Where does heritable variation come from?** Make and defend a claim distinguishing new combinations of existing alleles from new alleles caused by replication errors or environmental factors. **G4 · HS-LS3-2** | Students sort evidence cards about allele reshuffling during meiosis, viable DNA-copying errors, and environmentally caused DNA changes. They defend a classification and explain why a DNA change in a body cell is not ordinarily passed to offspring. | Chromosome cards; three evidence sets; claim-evidence-reasoning handout. | **Three cases:** Label each as “new allele combination,” “potential new allele,” or “not ordinarily passed to offspring,” and justify one classification using the cell lineage. | Use two sorting questions: “Did the DNA sequence change?” and “Could the affected cell contribute DNA to offspring?” | 5 retrieval / 10 visual model / 20 card sort / 15 written defense and discussion / 5 exit |
| **12. Can phenotype change without a DNA sequence change?** Analyze data linking gene expression to phenotype and revise a model to show where environmental conditions may influence the outcome. **G4, G5 · supports HS-LS1-1; contrasts with mutation in HS-LS3-2** | Students graph relative mRNA and pigment levels for genetically matched fictional plants grown under two light conditions. They revise their models and identify what the expression and pigment data support without claiming that the gene sequence changed. | Teacher-made dataset below; graph paper or spreadsheet; Day 1 and Day 5 models. | **Explain the contrast:** Two groups have the same tested DNA sequence but different mRNA and pigment levels. What explanation fits, and what is one thing the data do not establish? | Provide graphs with labeled axes and ask students to annotate the strongest comparison. | 5 launch / 10 data orientation / 20 graph and interpret / 15 model revision / 5 exit |
| **13. What makes genetic technology evidence useful?** Evaluate two sources about a genetic technology, identify a quantitative finding and its limitation, and explain who may be affected. **G6 · evaluating-information practice; ETS1.B connection** | Introduce one common case, such as gene-editing treatment for sickle cell disease or direct-to-consumer genetic testing. Students compare an evidence source with a stakeholder source, checking who was studied, what was measured, and what the data do not answer. | Two short, accessible source excerpts; evidence organizer; options include FDA announcements, MedlinePlus Genetics, and NIH/NHGRI fact sheets. | **Evidence audit:** Write one usable numerical finding, including what it measures and its denominator if given. Name one question the finding cannot answer. | Offer excerpts with headings and a glossary for terms such as *efficacy*, *eligibility*, *risk*, and *consent*. | 5 case hook / 10 source demo / 20 paired reading / 15 evidence comparison / 5 exit |
| **14. How do we weigh competing recommendations?** Defend a preliminary recommendation using evidence and respond fairly to a stakeholder counterargument. **G6 · argument from evidence; ETS1.B connection** | Groups compare two realistic policy options using criteria such as benefit, safety, access, and consent. Each student then drafts a recommendation, the strongest objection to it, and an evidence-based response or safeguard. | Case packet; stakeholder cards; two-option decision matrix; policy rubric. | **Claim and challenge:** State your recommendation, name the stakeholder most likely to challenge it, and give a specific reason they might. | Offer a silent written discussion as an alternative to speaking in the group deliberation. | 5 criteria review / 10 prep / 20 deliberation / 15 outline / 5 exit |
| **15. ### Ready-to-use datasets and free tools

- **Lessons 9–10: Simulated monohybrid counts.** For an `Aa × Aa` cross with complete dominance, the expected phenotype ratio is 3:1. Day 9 backup data: **56 dominant, 24 recessive** out of 80; expected **60 and 20**; χ² ≈ **1.07**. For Day 10, use **50 dominant, 30 recessive** out of 80; χ² ≈ **6.67**. With 1 degree of freedom and a supplied critical value of **3.84** at α = .05, students should conclude that the first dataset is **not inconsistent** with the model, while the second is **inconsistent** under the test assumptions. Neither result tells students *why* the counts differ.
- **Lesson 12: Fictional plant expression data.** Give students these paired values as **relative mRNA / pigment**: lower light, **2/3, 3/4, 2/4**; higher light, **7/9, 8/10, 9/11**. State that the groups have the same tested sequence at the pigment gene. The data support an association among light, expression, and pigment under these conditions; they do not establish the full causal mechanism.
- **Free classroom tools:** [LibreOffice Calc](https://www.libreoffice.org/discover/calc/) for tallying and graphing without student accounts; [HHMI BioInteractive](https://www.biointeractive.org/) for optional DNA and gene-expression visuals; [MedlinePlus Genetics](https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/) for accessible background; and [FDA press announcements](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/fda-newsroom/press-announcements) for public evidence summaries. Paper strips, coins, and graph paper work for every core activity.

## Analytic rubrics

Score each row separately: **4 = thorough, 3 = meets the target, 2 = developing, 1 = limited evidence.** Each assessment has four criteria for a total of **16 points**. A **3** describes the intended level of proficiency.

### Assessment 1 — Central Dogma Mutation Model

| Criterion | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Sequence model** | Accurately models replication, transcription, and translation for both versions; labels the template, codons, and point at which the variant changes the outcome. | Accurately traces both versions through DNA copying, mRNA, and amino acids; labels the main stages. | Models some stages correctly, but a strand, base-pairing, or decoding error changes the result. | Omits major stages or does not show a usable sequence-to-protein connection. |
| **Protein function and phenotype** | Uses sequence, activity, and phenotype evidence to explain the outcome; distinguishes a prediction from a measured result. | Uses sequence and supplied data to explain how the variant does or does not affect protein function and phenotype. | Cites some evidence but leaves a gap between sequence, protein function, and phenotype. | Gives an unsupported conclusion or assumes every DNA change changes phenotype. |
| **Heritability** | Explains how the affected cell lineage determines whether transmission is possible and distinguishes possible transmission from certainty. | Correctly explains whether the change could be inherited in the stated case, using the affected cell type or lineage. | Gives a plausible answer but an incomplete or inconsistent reason. | Confuses a change in a body cell with an inherited change, or gives no explanation. |
| **Revision and limitation** | Makes a meaningful evidence-based revision and identifies a specific limit that affects what can be concluded. | Shows one revision prompted by evidence and identifies one valid model limitation. | Shows a revision without a clear evidence link, or gives only a vague limitation. | Shows neither an evidence-based revision nor a valid limitation. |

### Assessment 2 — Family Inheritance Investigation

| Criterion | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Pedigree reasoning** | Defends the most likely pattern using multiple relationships, tests a plausible alternative, and distinguishes definite from possible genotypes. | Identifies the most likely pattern, supports it with pedigree evidence, and marks uncertain genotypes. | Identifies a plausible pattern, but evidence or genotype assignments are incomplete or inconsistent. | Gives a pattern without relevant evidence or misreads key relationships. |
| **Probability model** | Calculates the correct probability, states the parental genotype assumptions, and explains how unresolved genotypes could affect the prediction. | Uses an appropriate cross or probability model to calculate the correct conditional probability. | Uses an appropriate method but makes a consequential setup, calculation, or interpretation error. | Gives a probability that is unsupported or unrelated to the proposed cross. |
| **Statistical analysis** | Calculates expected counts and χ² correctly, interprets the result in context, and identifies a relevant assumption or limitation. | Calculates expected counts and χ² and correctly states whether the data are inconsistent with the predicted distribution. | Shows part of the calculation or compares counts correctly but misinterprets the test. | Does not make a valid observed-versus-expected comparison or conclusion. |
| **Family communication and inquiry** | Clearly explains risk and uncertainty without implying a guarantee; asks a focused DNA or chromosome question and identifies what evidence could answer it. | Explains the probability and its limits in plain language and asks a relevant question about DNA or chromosomes in inheritance. | Gives a family explanation that is unclear or overly certain, or asks only a broad question. | Gives a misleading family explanation and does not pose a relevant inheritance question. |

### Assessment 3 — Genetic Technology Policy Brief

| Criterion | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Recommendation and scientific accuracy** | Makes a specific, actionable recommendation with conditions or safeguards and accurately explains the relevant genetic mechanism and its limits. | Makes a clear recommendation and accurately explains the science needed to understand it. | Gives a broad recommendation or an incomplete scientific explanation. | Gives no clear recommendation or relies on a major scientific misconception. |
| **Evidence and source evaluation** | Synthesizes two or more sources, interprets a quantitative finding in context, and explains a source or data limitation that affects the recommendation. | Uses at least two sources and accurately interprets at least one quantitative finding in support of the recommendation. | Uses too little evidence, drops in a number without interpreting it, or misreads a source. | Relies on unsupported assertions or substantially misrepresents the evidence. |
| **Stakeholders and trade-offs** | Weighs competing stakeholder priorities, explains who bears a risk or cost, and proposes a safeguard tied to an unintended consequence. | Compares at least two stakeholder perspectives and explains a plausible unintended consequence connected to the case. | Lists perspectives or consequences but does not explain the trade-off. | Omits stakeholder perspectives or relevant consequences. |
| **Counterargument and response** | Presents the strongest reasonable objection fairly and uses evidence to rebut it or meaningfully qualify the recommendation. | Presents a plausible counterargument and responds with relevant evidence or reasoning. | Mentions an objection but gives a weak or unsupported response. | Omits a counterargument or dismisses it without reasoning. |

## Student-facing “I can” checklist

For each statement, mark **Not yet / With help / On my own** and jot down a lesson or piece of work that shows what you can do.

- **G1:** I can use a model to explain how DNA is copied and how its sequence helps determine the protein a cell makes and what that protein does.
- **G2:** I can ask how DNA and chromosomes explain an inheritance pattern, use crosses and pedigrees to make predictions, and tell which genotypes are certain or only possible.
- **G3:** I can compare predicted and observed trait frequencies and explain what the statistics do—and do not—tell me about an inheritance model.
- **G4:** I can explain how new allele combinations and mutations create variation, when that variation can be inherited, and how gene expression can affect a trait without a DNA sequence change.
- **G5:** I can revise a genotype-to-phenotype model using new evidence and explain one thing the model cannot show.
- **G6:** I can defend a recommendation about genetic testing or gene editing using evidence and explain how the benefits, risks, and trade-offs differ for the people affected.

### Create the files

1. Open [script.google.com](https://script.google.com/) and select **New project**.
2. Replace the starter code with the script below. Select **`buildWeek1Genetics`**, click **Run**, and authorize access to Slides, Docs, and Drive.

|---|---|

function makeDeck(folder, name, slideData) {
  const deck = SlidesApp.create(name);
  const first = deck.getSlides()[0];
  const width = deck.getPageWidth();
  const height = deck.getPageHeight();
  slideData.forEach((data, i) => {
    const slide = deck.appendSlide(SlidesApp.PredefinedLayout.BLANK);
    slide.getBackground().setSolidFill('#F5F8FB');
    const title = slide.insertTextBox(data[0], 32, 24, width - 64, 58);
    title.getText().getTextStyle()
      .setFontFamily('Arial').setFontSize(28).setBold(true)
      .setForegroundColor('#16354F');
    const body = slide.insertTextBox(data.slice(1).join('\n\n'),
      32, 96, width - 64, height - 139);
    body.getText().getTextStyle()
      .setFontFamily('Arial').setFontSize(20).setForegroundColor('#202B33');
    const footer = slide.insertTextBox(name + '  |  ' + (i + 1),
      32, height - 31, width - 64, 21);
    footer.getText().getTextStyle()
      .setFontFamily('Arial').setFontSize(10).setForegroundColor('#45627A');
  });
  first.remove();
  const id = deck.getId();
  deck.saveAndClose();
  saveMasterAndPdf(folder, id, name);
}

function makeDoc(folder, name, pages) {
  const doc = DocumentApp.create(name);
  const body = doc.getBody();
  body.clear();
  body.setPageWidth(612).setPageHeight(792)
    .setMarginTop(40).setMarginBottom(40)
    .setMarginLeft(46).setMarginRight(46);
  pages.forEach((lines, pageIndex) => {
    if (pageIndex > 0) body.appendPageBreak();
    lines.forEach((line, i) => {
      const mono = line.charAt(0) === '@';
      const text = mono ? line.slice(1) : line;
      const p = body.appendParagraph(text || ' ');
      p.setSpacingBefore(0).setSpacingAfter(
        i === 0 ? 9 : mono ? 2 : text ? 5 : 1
      ).setLineSpacing(1.08);
      p.editAsText()
        .setFontFamily(mono ? 'Courier New' : 'Arial')
        .setFontSize(i === 0 ? 17 : mono ? 10 : 10.5)
        .setBold(i === 0);
    });
  });
  const id = doc.getId();
  doc.saveAndClose();
  saveMasterAndPdf(folder, id, name);
}

function saveMasterAndPdf(folder, id, name) {
  const master = DriveApp.getFileById(id);
  master.moveTo(folder);
  folder.createFile(master.getAs(MimeType.PDF).setName(name + '.pdf'));
}

TITLE
Which plant makes more pigment?

BODY
Plant A: dark purple leaves. Plant B: pale purple leaves.
Both were grown under the same classroom conditions.
Notice one difference. Ask one question about its cause.

SPEAKER NOTES — 0–8 min
• 0–3: Read the two plant descriptions. Ask students to record one
  observation without explaining its cause.
• 3–8: Have pairs compare observations and write a question. If someone
  says “different DNA,” ask: “Did we observe that, or is it a hypothesis?”


SLIDE — L1 — Slide 2
TITLE
Evidence: an enzyme helps make pigment

BODY
An enzyme is a protein that helps a chemical reaction happen.
Plant A: enzyme activity 100; pigment 8.0.
Plant B: enzyme activity 28; pigment 2.5.
Activity and pigment are reported in relative units.

SPEAKER NOTES — 8–18 min
• 8–12: Define enzyme and pigment. Point out that activity and pigment
  are separate measurements; compare each measure across plants.
• 12–18: Ask students to cite both comparisons. Check: “Which arrow
  do these numbers support? Did we measure DNA?”


SLIDE — L1 — Slide 3
TITLE
Build an initial model

BODY
Connect DNA → protein → pigment → leaf color.
Explain one arrow using today’s evidence.
Put a ? on a link that the data do not yet explain.

SPEAKER NOTES — 18–40 min
• 18–23: Hand out the standard or guided template. Model one arrow
  label: “Higher enzyme activity may help the plant make more pigment.”
• 23–40: Circulate. Ask each pair to point to a data-supported arrow
  and put a ? on one link they cannot yet explain.


SLIDE — L1 — Slide 4
TITLE
Compare, then exit

BODY
Compare models: Which arrow is best supported? Why?
Exit ticket: Explain one arrow and mark one unresolved link.

SPEAKER NOTES — 40–55 min
• 40–50: Partners compare their strongest arrows and unresolved links.
  Have students date and save this first model for Thursday.

  a genuine uncertainty, such as whether the plants differ in DNA.

SLIDE — L2 — Slide 1
TITLE
What rule makes a copy possible?

BODY
Learning target: Use base pairing to model DNA replication.
Predict the partner for each base: A, T, C, G.

SPEAKER NOTES — 0–5 min
• 0–2: Ask students to write the four partners without using the strips.
• 2–5: Check A–T and C–G. Ask: “If you know one strand, what lets you
  predict the other?”


SLIDE — L2 — Slide 2
TITLE
Copy both original strands

BODY
Separate the two original paper strands.
Build one new partner for each original strand: A pairs with T; C pairs with G.
Label OLD and NEW. Each finished DNA molecule has one of each.

SPEAKER NOTES — 5–35 min

  Keep the 3′ and 5′ labels visible as you align the bases.

  partner to identify the OLD and NEW strands in both molecules.


SLIDE — L2 — Slide 3
TITLE
When does a copying error matter?

BODY
Compare an accurate copy with a copy that has a mismatch.

Would a lasting change confined to a mature leaf cell usually reach offspring? Why?

SPEAKER NOTES — 35–50 min
• 35–42: Have one partner swap a NEW tile and the other find and fix
  the mismatch. Clarify that a copying mismatch can be corrected.

  that change to reach offspring through seeds?”


SLIDE — L2 — Slide 4
TITLE
5-minute exit ticket

BODY
Check a proposed complementary strand.
Then explain whether a change confined to one leaf would ordinarily be inherited.

SPEAKER NOTES — 50–55 min

TITLE
Two different jobs

BODY
Replication copies DNA into DNA.
Transcription uses a DNA template to make RNA.
Translation uses mRNA codons to build an amino acid chain.

5-minute exit ticket

BODY

• 50–53: Students name one piece of evidence for each claim.
